reference.source: Standard endocrinology and critical care reference texts and adrenal disorder consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A potentially life-threatening cause of acute primary adrenal insufficiency, since destruction of both glands abolishes cortisol and aldosterone production
Should be suspected in an unwell patient with new abdominal, flank or back pain, hypotension, fever and unexplained clinical deterioration
Common precipitants include severe sepsis (classically meningococcal, Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), major stress or surgery, coagulopathy and anticoagulant therapy
Antiphospholipid syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia are important thrombotic causes and may be the presenting feature of these conditions
Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and eosinophilia are supportive biochemical clues to evolving adrenal insufficiency
CT or MRI shows bilateral adrenal enlargement with high-attenuation or evolving blood signal, distinguishing haemorrhage from tumour
Because Addisonian crisis can be rapidly fatal, empirical glucocorticoid replacement should not await definitive confirmation when suspicion is high
reference.pathophysiology: The adrenal gland has a rich arterial supply that drains through a limited venous system into a single central vein, creating a vascular watershed that predisposes to haemorrhage and infarction under stress. Surges in ACTH increase adrenal arterial inflow while venous outflow is constrained, and superimposed thrombosis, coagulopathy, anticoagulation, platelet consumption, or endotoxin-mediated vascular injury in sepsis precipitate bleeding into the gland. When haemorrhage is bilateral and extensive, the cortex is destroyed, cutting off cortisol and aldosterone output and producing acute primary adrenal insufficiency with hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Acute adrenal insufficiency from other causes (e.g. autoimmune, abrupt steroid withdrawal)
Sepsis or septic shock without adrenal haemorrhage
Acute abdomen from other retroperitoneal pathology
additionalInvestigations: Paired morning cortisol with ACTH, and a short synacthen test where feasible, to confirm adrenal insufficiency
Serum sodium, potassium, glucose and renal function to assess mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid loss
Non-contrast and contrast CT or MRI of the adrenals to demonstrate bilateral haemorrhage
Coagulation screen, platelet count and testing for antiphospholipid antibodies and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Septic workup including blood cultures when infection is suspected
Follow-up imaging to monitor resolution and exclude an underlying mass
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability and shock indicating adrenal (Addisonian) crisis
Hyperkalaemia with hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia signalling combined hormone loss
Rapid clinical deterioration in a septic or anticoagulated patient
Evidence of ongoing retroperitoneal bleeding or expanding haematoma
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on how quickly adrenal insufficiency is recognised and treated and on the severity of the underlying illness; delayed steroid replacement can be fatal, whereas prompt treatment allows recovery, though some patients are left with permanent adrenal insufficiency requiring lifelong replacement.
pitfalls: Delaying glucocorticoid replacement while awaiting confirmatory hormonal results
Attributing hypotension solely to sepsis and missing coexisting adrenal insufficiency
Overlooking an underlying prothrombotic disorder such as antiphospholipid syndrome
Mistaking haemorrhagic adrenal enlargement for a primary adrenal tumour
references: Consensus guidance on diagnosis and management of adrenal insufficiency
management: Immediate intravenous hydrocortisone for suspected acute adrenal crisis, given empirically before biochemical confirmation
Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation with correction of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia

Treat the precipitant, including antimicrobials for sepsis such as meningococcal disease, and manage the coagulopathy, switching from heparin to an alternative anticoagulant in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Long-term anticoagulation and specialist input where antiphospholipid syndrome is the underlying thrombotic cause
Transition to maintenance oral glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone as the patient stabilises
Endocrinology referral with follow-up imaging to confirm resolution and identify persistent adrenal insufficiency
Educate on sick-day dosing and provide a steroid emergency card and parenteral hydrocortisone for those left with lasting insufficiency
